newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leaders talk but impeachment case goes on.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leaders talk but impeachment case goes on.

text.p: The Constitutional Court in Belarus has begun to review a move by members of parliament to impeach President Alexander Lukashenko but further talks seemed likely on Wednesday which could help to defuse the political crisis.

In the first sign tension might be easing after weeks of mounting confrontation, a senior political source in the former Soviet republic said Lukashenko had expressed a readiness to compromise, possibly dropping his bid for sweeping new powers in exchange for parliament abandoning its attempt to impeach him.
Belarus state television later said, however, that the court, which like parliament has already clashed with the president, had decided to begin reviewing the impeachment move.
And Lukashenko's chief-of-staff, Mikhail Myasnikovich, told Russian Television there was no question of him dropping his plan to seek popular approval for a new constitution.

The political source said Lukashenko, who also spoke to Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin by telephone, made the offer of compromise in a meeting with Valery Tikhinya, president of the Constitutional Court.
"But let's see what happens tomorrow," the source added.
There were reports of more planned talks, including with top Russian officials, whose concern has become increasingly evident. The reports could not be immediately confirmed.

It is far from clear that anti-Lukashenko deputies can assemble the two-thirds majority in parliament needed to remove the president, who has organised a referendum for Sunday seeking approval for powers which his opponents decry as "dictatorial".
Lukashenko, who controls the security forces and most of the media and who enjoys considerable support among the mostly rural population of 10 million, has vowed to override any opposition.

However, Myasnikovich said after meeting Semyon Sharetsky, the parliamentary speaker and a leader of opposition to the president: "There are absolutely no grounds to stir up fear and say we will settle this conflict by some sort of use of force."
State television said Lukashenko would meet "representatives of the central authorities" on Wednesday but gave no details.
Lukashenko's spokesman could not confirm a report that the president would meet Sharetsky.

Russian news agency RIA quoted Sharetsky saying late on Tuesday that he expected to meet the speakers of the two chambers of the Russian parliament on Wednesday in the Russian city of Smolensk, close to the Belarus border.
Sharetsky was also quoted as saying he could not rule out Lukashenko and Chernomyrdin joining in the talks. Russian and Belarus officials were not available to comment on the report.
The hint of a compromise from Lukashenko came after a day of mounting alarm among neighbouring states at the confrontation.
France expressed concern among Western states that the referendum was illegal. There were strong hints of disquiet at Lukashenko's plans from Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine.
But there were signs that intervention by Russia may have been crucial in persuading Lukashenko to back off even though his parliamentary opponents were in disarray.
Interfax news agency quoted a source close to Lukashenko as saying Chernomyrdin had "expressed concern" and voiced support for efforts to settle the conflict and stabilise the situation.
Interfax said Lukashenko might fly to Moscow for talks.
A Kremlin spokesman said earlier on Tuesday President Boris Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin "expressed alarm about rising tension" and hoped that common sense and compromise would prevail.
Lukashenko has ignored the current constitution and rulings by the Constitutional Court in declaring that the referendum, for which early voting has already started, must be binding.
The 42-year-old leader has scorned Western criticism but is heavily dependent on the political winds blowing from Moscow. He and Yeltsin agreed in April to unite in a "community".
Lukashenko is seeking authority to extend his term by more than two years and widen his powers over all institutions.
